question: An Azure SQL Database API distinguishes an omitted optional key from a key whose value is JSON null or an empty string. It must include the code and numeric zero but omit the SQL NULL comment value. Which constructor satisfies that contract?

question: On SQL Server 2022, dbo.Link has int columns FromId and ToId and can contain cycles. The query must enumerate walks from node 1 using at most three edges. Some retained path strings exceed 20 characters, but all fit nvarchar(200). The shown CTE has a type mismatch and relies on an outer depth filter. Which repair makes the types agree and bounds recursion without truncating valid paths?

answerChoices.text: Cast the anchor path to nvarchar(200), but leave depth filtering only in the outer SELECT.
Cast the recursive path to nvarchar(20) and add WHERE r.Depth < 3 to the recursive member.
Leave the path casts unchanged and add OPTION (MAXRECURSION 3) to the outer SELECT.
Cast the anchor path to nvarchar(200) and add WHERE r.Depth < 3 to the recursive member.

explanation: Match the anchor's path type to the recursive nvarchar(200) type and stop producing rows after depth three.
deepExplanation: Recursive CTE columns must have the same types in anchor and recursive members, including string width. A predicate on the recursive input depth prevents a depth-three row from generating a depth-four row. Filtering final output does not terminate a cyclic recursion, and MAXRECURSION is an error safeguard rather than a request to return a truncated walk.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: This fixes the type mismatch but leaves cycles able to keep generating deeper rows; the output filter is not a recursive termination predicate.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: The types agree but valid paths longer than 20 characters can be truncated.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: A recursion limit does not fix incompatible column types or implement the requested terminating walk logic.

documentationTitles: Organize queries with common table expressions
codeSnippet:
WITH Walk AS
(
    SELECT CAST(1 AS int) AS NodeId, 0 AS Depth,
           CAST(N'1' AS nvarchar(20)) AS NodePath
    UNION ALL
    SELECT l.ToId, r.Depth + 1,
           CAST(r.NodePath + N'/' + CONVERT(nvarchar(11), l.ToId)
                AS nvarchar(200))
    FROM Walk AS r
    JOIN dbo.Link AS l ON l.FromId = r.NodeId
)
SELECT NodeId, Depth, NodePath
FROM Walk
WHERE Depth <= 3;
verificationNotes: PASS 3 independently tested natural termination, narrow common types and MAXRECURSION as alternate repairs. d alone both compiles with adequate width and ceases generation after three edges. A repeated-node walk is allowed; no unasked simple-path or deduplication rule was imported. The familiar MAXRECURSION guard is not a request for a successful partial query. Compared actual direct-006 alternatives and source hierarchy examples. Static code review only.
confidenceReason: High for the bounded recursive repair: documented type equality and empty-member termination produce a direct induction over depths zero through three.

question: A SQL Server 2022 report shows meter readings from @Cutoff onward, but each delta must compare with that meter's immediately preceding reading even when it is before @Cutoff. Values are nonnull, can rise or fall, and (ReadingTime, ReadingId) uniquely orders each meter. The first displayed delta is unexpectedly NULL although an older reading exists. Which change fixes the rowset used by LAG?

answerChoices.text: Keep the WHERE clause in place and give LAG a default of zero.
Compute LAG in an inner query over the complete relevant meter history, then apply the cutoff in an outer query.
Keep the WHERE clause in place and replace LAG with LEAD.
Keep the WHERE clause in place and increase LAG's offset from one to two.

explanation: Calculate the preceding-reading value before applying the display-only time filter.
deepExplanation: At this query level, WHERE removes older rows before the SELECT-list window expression is evaluated. LAG cannot see a row that is no longer in its partition. An inner calculation over the required history followed by an outer report filter preserves the previous-reading comparison without displaying the older rows. No particular physical plan or IGNORE NULLS behavior is assumed.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: Zero is not the missing historical reading and fabricates a different delta rather than restoring that row to the window.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: LEAD looks forward, not to the immediately preceding reading.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: A larger offset does not restore filtered-out history and requests the wrong predecessor distance.

subskill: Write queries that include window functions
codeSnippet:
SELECT MeterId, ReadingTime, ReadingId,
       Reading - LAG(Reading) OVER
           (PARTITION BY MeterId ORDER BY ReadingTime, ReadingId) AS Delta
FROM dbo.MeterReading
WHERE ReadingTime >= @Cutoff;
verificationNotes: PASS 3 constructed a falling-value counterexample to the zero default and traced direction and offset alternatives. b fixes the logical rowset; this is not an instruction to force materialization or override optimizer execution order. The word preceding is bound to the supplied unique ascending order. Actual SELECT and LAG bodies were combined with the genuine teaching references; older approval was not used as proof. Distinct from nearby running-total and ranking items.
confidenceReason: High for the query-boundary repair: logical SELECT ordering plus LAG's own offset/default contract make the alternatives falsifiable with a three-row example.

question: A SQL Server 2025 workflow explicitly uses the Preview fuzzy-string functions. It retains all bounded, nonnull candidate name pairs, but computes EDIT_DISTANCE(LeftName, RightName, 2) for final ranking. Several distinct pairs receive 3. Replace the capped distance with EDIT_DISTANCE_SIMILARITY and order that score descending.
Set maximum_distance to 0 so every nonidentical pair is assigned a common small value.

question: On SQL Server 2022, dbo.Test has a nullable Result column. A batch is eligible only if it has at least one test and every test has Result = 'pass'. NULL must count as not passed. Which predicate returns exactly the eligible batches, including correct treatment of empty batches and mixed results?

answerChoices.text: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.Test t WHERE t.BatchId = b.BatchId) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.Test t WHERE t.BatchId = b.BatchId AND t.Result <> 'pass')
EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.Test t WHERE t.BatchId = b.BatchId AND t.Result = 'pass') AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.Test t WHERE t.BatchId = b.BatchId AND t.Result IS NULL)
EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.Test t WHERE t.BatchId = b.BatchId) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.Test t WHERE t.BatchId = b.BatchId AND (t.Result <> 'pass' OR t.Result IS NULL))
NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.Test t WHERE t.BatchId = b.BatchId AND (t.Result <> 'pass' OR t.Result IS NULL))

explanation: Require at least one related row and exclude any related row that is non-pass or NULL.
deepExplanation: NOT EXISTS expresses that no counterexample exists, but it is also true for a batch with no tests. A separate EXISTS closes that empty-batch gap. In the counterexample predicate, Result <> 'pass' does not identify NULL, so IS NULL must be explicit. Both subqueries remain correlated to the current batch.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: A NULL result does not satisfy the <> comparison, so this admits batches whose only problematic results are NULL.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: This admits a batch containing both pass and fail results, provided no result is NULL.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: An empty batch has no counterexample and therefore qualifies, contrary to the required at-least-one-test condition.

verificationNotes: PASS 3 used concrete empty, NULL-only, pass-only, fail-only, pass/fail and pass/NULL cases. c alone matches all requirements. EXISTS(SELECT NULL) was deliberately separated from a nullable WHERE comparison; the latter support comes from Subqueries' inequality example and is recorded as static derivation. Negative wording is essential to the stated business rule, not answer hiding. The repeated BatchId correlations prevent a separate scope error. No forced physical-plan claim or live SQL execution.
confidenceReason: High for the logical result: three minimal counterexample batches independently defeat a, b and d; c enforces all stated conditions.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: The product explicitly permits an outer CATCH to handle compilation errors arising at a lower execution level.
